tec-mfa.summary: A second proof at sign-in, beyond the password, so a stolen password alone does not open an account.
tec-mfa.protects: Email, remote access (VPN, ZTNA, VDI), admin consoles, cloud and SaaS apps, and payment journeys. It counters phishing, password spraying, credential stuffing and reuse of leaked passwords.
tec-mfa.placement: A cloud identity service (identity provider) in front of all apps, plus a RADIUS or agent connector on-premise for VPN, servers and legacy apps. The IAM team owns it; the service desk owns enrolment and recovery.
tec-mfa.how: The identity provider asks for a second factor based on policy: who the user is, the app, the device and the risk. Phishing-resistant factors (FIDO2 security keys, passkeys, smart cards) bind the login to the real site, so a fake site cannot replay it. Weaker factors (SMS, voice, simple push) still help, but can be phished or fatigued.
pareto: Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2 keys or passkeys) for every admin and every privileged role first.
MFA on remote access, email and every internet-facing app before internal apps.
Number matching on push approvals, and SMS only as a last-resort fallback.
Block legacy authentication protocols that cannot do MFA (for example basic auth to mail).
A secure, identity-verified recovery process at the service desk, because attackers target the reset.

tec-mfa.architecture: Users and devices sign in to the identity provider (cloud service, often the same one that runs SSO). Apps trust it through SAML or OIDC. tec-waf.summary: A filter in front of web applications that blocks common attacks (injection, cross-site scripting, known exploits) before they reach the app.
tec-waf.protects: Internet-facing websites, portals and APIs, and the data behind them. It counters the OWASP Top 10 classes, known CVE exploits, scanners, and some bots and layer-7 floods. It buys time while code is fixed (virtual patching).
tec-waf.placement: Inline on the path to every internet-facing app: either a cloud WAAP service (DNS points to the provider, which forwards clean traffic) or an appliance or virtual WAF in the DMZ, in an HA pair, behind the edge firewall and in front of the load balancers. Network security operates it; app owners own the tuning.
tec-waf.how: Each request is checked against signatures (for example the OWASP Core Rule Set), the app's learned normal behaviour and reputation data. Bad requests are blocked, challenged or logged. Start in detection mode, tune false positives with app teams, then switch to blocking.
pareto: Every internet-facing app behind the WAF, with origin servers reachable only from the WAF.
Blocking mode on a tuned managed rule set (OWASP CRS or vendor rules) within 30-60 days.
Virtual patching of new critical CVEs within 24-48 hours.
Rate limits on login, OTP and search endpoints.
WAF logs into the SIEM with alerts on blocked attack spikes.

tec-waf.architecture: Internet -> anti-DDoS scrubbing -> WAF (cloud edge or DMZ appliance pair) -> load balancer -> web/app tier. tec-pam.summary: A controlled gate for administrator and other powerful accounts: passwords are locked in a vault, access is granted only when needed, and sessions are recorded.
tec-pam.protects: Domain admin, root, database admin, network device, cloud console, core banking and service accounts. It counters credential theft, lateral movement, insider misuse and vendor misuse of remote admin access.
tec-pam.placement: Vault and session servers in a dedicated management zone of the data centre (with a DR copy), or as a SaaS with on-premise connectors. Admins reach targets only through it, from hardened admin workstations. The IAM team owns it; system owners approve access.
tec-pam.how: Privileged credentials are discovered, moved into an encrypted vault and rotated automatically. Admins check out access through a portal or proxy after MFA and approval, often just-in-time for a limited period, without seeing the password. Sessions are recorded and commands can be filtered, and all activity goes to the SIEM.
pareto: Discover and vault all domain admin, root, DBA and network device credentials, with automatic rotation.
All vendor and third-party admin access only through PAM, recorded, with approval.
Phishing-resistant MFA on the PAM portal itself.
Just-in-time access instead of standing admin rights for the most powerful roles.
Session recording reviewed for critical systems, and alerts to the SOC on risky commands.

tec-iam.summary: One system that decides who gets which access, grants it automatically when people join or move, reviews it regularly and removes it when they leave.
tec-iam.protects: All applications and data, by keeping access right-sized. It counters orphan accounts of leavers, privilege creep, toxic combinations (segregation of duties breaks) and audit findings on access reviews.
tec-iam.placement: A central identity service (SaaS or on-premise in the server zone) connected to HR as the source of truth and to the directory and applications through connectors. The IAM team runs it; managers and app owners approve and review.
tec-iam.how: HR events (joiner, mover, leaver) trigger automatic account creation, change and removal using roles and rules. Users request extra access through a portal, with approvals and segregation-of-duties checks. Managers and app owners certify access on a schedule, and unapproved access is removed.
pareto: HR system as the single source of truth, with leavers disabled everywhere within 24 hours.
Connectors to the 10-15 most critical applications first (core banking, email, VPN, finance, HR).
Quarterly access reviews for critical apps and privileged roles, with automatic removal on 'revoke'.
A small set of birthright roles per department instead of copy-a-colleague access.
Orphan and dormant account clean-up every month.

tec-sast.summary: Automated and manual testing of your own software for security flaws, in code (SAST), in open-source parts (SCA) and in the running app (DAST), before release.
tec-sast.protects: In-house and vendor-built applications, APIs and mobile apps, and the customer data they handle. It counters injection, broken access control, insecure libraries, leaked secrets in code and misconfiguration.
tec-sast.placement: Inside the build pipeline (CI/CD) and developer tools for SAST, SCA and secrets scanning; DAST runs against test or staging environments. The security testing lead owns it; development teams fix findings.
tec-sast.how: SAST reads the source code and flags risky patterns; SCA lists open-source libraries and their known vulnerabilities; DAST attacks the running app like an outsider. A release gate blocks builds with critical findings unless an exception is approved. Manual code review and penetration testing cover what tools miss, such as business logic.

tec-api.summary: Tools that find every API you expose, test it for the API-specific flaws, and watch live API traffic for abuse.
tec-api.protects: Customer and transaction data behind APIs used by mobile apps, partners, fintechs, account aggregators and internal services. It counters broken object-level authorisation (one customer reading another's data), broken authentication, excessive data exposure, shadow and zombie APIs, and business-logic abuse.
tec-api.placement: Out of band, reading copies of API traffic from the API gateway, load balancer, WAF or cloud logs, plus scanners in the pipeline. Blocking is done through the WAF or API gateway. The security architect owns it; API owners fix findings.
tec-api.how: The platform builds an inventory of APIs from live traffic and code, flags sensitive data and unauthenticated endpoints, and compares calls with the API specification. It learns normal behaviour per user and per endpoint and alerts on attacks such as enumeration of object IDs. Testing modules run the OWASP API Top 10 checks before release.
pareto: A complete API inventory, including undocumented (shadow) and old versions, with an owner for each.
Object-level authorisation tests (OWASP API1) on every API that returns customer data.
All external APIs through a gateway with authentication, rate limits and schema validation.

Retire old API versions on a fixed schedule.

tec-bot.summary: Protection that tells humans from automated scripts on login, OTP, payment and sign-up journeys, plus runtime self-protection inside the application.
tec-bot.protects: Customer accounts, OTP and SMS budgets, offers and inventory, and the application itself. It counters credential stuffing, account takeover, fake account creation, OTP and SMS pumping, scraping, card testing and, with RASP, exploitation of code flaws at run time.

Bad bots are blocked, slowed, challenged or fed decoy content, while good bots (search engines, partners) are allowed. RASP watches calls inside the app (such as database queries) and blocks an exploit as it happens.

clauses: Right to audit: the organisation, its auditors and the regulator (RBI, SEBI or IRDAI as applicable) may audit the provider and its sub-contractors, on site or remotely.
RBI Master Direction on Outsourcing of IT Services (2023) applies to regulated entities: due diligence, a board-approved outsourcing policy, concentration risk, and no outsourcing of accountability.
CERT-In directions of 28 April 2022: the provider reports cyber incidents to the organisation fast enough to meet the 6-hour CERT-In deadline, and keeps its relevant logs for 180 days.
Exit and transition: export of all configuration, policies and logs in an open format, and transition support for at least 90 days at contract end.
DPDP Act 2023: device and behaviour signals can be personal data; a lawful basis, notice and minimisation are needed, and the provider acts as a data processor.
RBI Authentication Mechanisms for Digital Payment Transactions Directions, 2025: bot and risk signals can support risk-based checks, but do not replace the required two factors.

tec-bot.architecture: Customer browser or mobile app (SDK collects signals) -> CDN/WAAP edge with bot management (scores and enforces) -> WAF -> login, OTP and payment services. RASP agents run inside the app servers. Decisions and signals go to the fraud engine and SIEM; the fraud team tunes policies.
kpis: Credential-stuffing logins blocked versus account takeovers that still happen
OTP/SMS spend from bot traffic (falling)
Legitimate customers challenged or blocked (below an agreed rate)
Share of critical journeys protected (target 100%)
pitfalls: Protecting the website but not the mobile app API
CAPTCHAs that block real customers on slow networks
No joint ownership with the fraud team
Relying on IP blocking alone, which residential proxies defeat
